hints: Look very carefully at carbon 1 on the right side of each ring, that is the anomeric carbon where alpha and beta forms differ, then compare the rest of the OH positions.
Remember beta-glucose has the OH on carbon 1 in the same up position as the CH2OH group, while alpha-glucose has it down, all other OH groups stay in the glucose pattern.
walkthrough:
**Recall what makes glucose, glucose**

All four rings have the formula $C_6H_{12}O_6$, so you cannot use the formula alone. You must look at the positions of the OH groups around the ring. Glucose has a very specific pattern of OH groups on carbons 2, 3 and 4.

Think of alpha and beta glucose as twins that are identical everywhere except at carbon 1.

**Compare diagrams 1 and 2**

In both 1 and 2, the OH groups on the bottom and left side match the glucose pattern. The only difference is on carbon 1 on the right. In 1 the OH is up, in the same direction as the $CH_2OH$, and in 2 the OH is down.

That is exactly the difference between beta-glucose and alpha-glucose.

**Check why 3 and 4 are not glucose**

In diagram 3, look at the second carbon from the right on the bottom. Both OH groups point down together. In diagram 4, look at the left side and bottom. The OH pattern is flipped compared to glucose. These different arrangements make them different hexose isomers, not glucose.

So only 1 and 2 show glucose molecules.

options.A: Correct. 1 is beta-glucose and 2 is alpha-glucose. They share the glucose OH pattern and differ only at carbon 1.
options.B: Incorrect. 1 is glucose but 3 is not, as its OH on carbon 2 is in the wrong position for glucose.
options.C: Incorrect. 2 is glucose but 3 is not, as 3 has a different arrangement of OH groups on the lower carbons.
options.D: Incorrect. Neither 3 nor 4 is glucose, both show a different hexose with OH groups in non-glucose positions.
